title: High School Sophomore Wins $10,000 for Tongue-Controlled Wheelchair Interface
summary:
Imagine controlling a computer or wheelchair without lifting a finger — just by moving your tongue and blinking. That's the reality of Tonguage, a project by Holly Tang, a sophomore at Wilson High School in Hacienda Heights, California. Her invention earned her the top prize of $10,000 in the 2026 IEEE Presidents' Scholarship competition, held at the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF) in Phoenix.

Tonguage is a noninvasive, computer-vision-based human-machine interface. It uses a standard laptop camera to track the user's tongue position and eye blinks. The tongue acts as a directional cursor, while blinks serve as mouse clicks. The system also includes face-tracking to verify that commands come from the intended user, ignoring anyone else in the camera's frame — a critical safety feature for wheelchair navigation.

Tang was motivated by a visit to a rehabilitation center, where she saw the challenges faced by people with mobility impairments. She deliberately designed Tonguage to work with affordable, readily available cameras rather than costly specialized hardware. "Mobility conditions don't discriminate," she said. "They can affect anyone of any income, gender, and socioeconomic status."

Beyond basic tasks, Tang emphasized the importance of fun. "We're so focused on trying to give people autonomy over just basic human tasks that we often leave out things like gaming," she said. "They deserve the freedom to play games and enjoy entertainment as well." Her system can also control robotic arms and other assistive technologies.

The IEEE Presidents' Scholarship, established by the IEEE Foundation, recognizes high school students with exceptional grasp of engineering and computer science. Second place went to Partap Sidhu for his mind-controlled lower-limb exoskeleton, and third place to Calvin Shang Hung for a rough-terrain robot. Tang plans to pursue biomedical engineering, and she credits her success to empathy: "Empathy is hard to teach in a classroom, but it can be learned through experience."
why_it_matters: Tonguage suggests that independence technology need not be locked behind costly devices; with a basic camera and clever software, mobility tools could become far more accessible to people across different incomes and regions.

background_read: The Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF) is the world's largest pre-college science competition, gathering thousands of student finalists from more than 60 countries each year.

The IEEE Presidents' Scholarship is run by the IEEE Foundation, the charitable arm of IEEE (the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, a global professional organization for engineers and computer scientists).

Assistive technology already includes eye-tracking and sip-and-puff systems, but many require expensive calibration or specialized equipment, leaving a gap in affordability for many people with mobility impairments.
Computer vision, which allows ordinary cameras to interpret what they see, has advanced enough to track small movements such as tongue position and eye blinks on standard laptop hardware.

Holly Tang, a sophomore at Wilson High School in Hacienda Heights, California, created Tonguage after visiting a rehabilitation center; second- and third-place projects also focused on assistive robotics.

perspectives.description: For people with mobility impairments, Tonguage could lower costs and make independence easier to obtain. Its focus on gaming and entertainment also treats users as full people with social and recreational needs, not just patients.

Safety and reliability remain concerns because a standard camera must correctly read subtle tongue motions and blinks in different lighting and environments. If face-tracking fails or mistakes another person's movement for a command, a wheelchair could move unexpectedly.

The project reflects a broader shift in assistive technology: moving from expensive, specialized hardware toward software that works with devices people already own. The IEEE competition results show that student engineers are increasingly focused on human-centered robotics.

Before Tonguage could be widely used, it would need testing with many different users, lighting conditions, and assistive devices. Future steps could include integrating with commercial wheelchair controllers and working with rehabilitation clinics to refine safety and usability.
